title: Berakhot 2a–3a: The Evening Shema
bigQuestion: How does the Talmud turn one short question about the evening prayer into a whole way of reading?

story.title: Where Does the Teacher Stand?
story.kicker: The Talmud's very first question is not about the answer. It is about where the question came from.
paragraphs: A student opens a printed volume of the Babylonian Talmud to its first page. The page number is not 1. It is 2a, because printers counted the title page as page one. In the center sits a short block of Hebrew. That block is the Mishnah, a law code edited around the year 200 CE. Its first line asks a practical question: from what time may a person say the Shema in the evening?

The Shema is a prayer built from verses in Deuteronomy. Rabbinic tradition holds that it is said twice a day, at night and in the morning. The Mishnah gives three answers about the evening time. Rabbi Eliezer says one thing. The Sages say another. Rabban Gamliel says a third. No one is silenced, and all three views stay on the page.

Then the Gemara begins. The Gemara is the long discussion that later teachers built around the Mishnah. Its first words do not ask which answer is right. They ask something stranger: where does the tanna stand? A tanna is a teacher of the Mishnah. The Gemara wants to know what the teacher already assumed when he asked "from what time."

That small question opens the whole book. It says that every rule rests on something earlier, and that a reader should dig for it. Students have started their Talmud study on this page for centuries. In this chapter you will read it closely, move by move, in translation.
story.think: Why might a book of law begin by asking where a question comes from instead of giving a rule?

lessons.title: A Tractate Called Blessings
lessons.mainIdea: Berakhot, meaning "blessings," is the first tractate of the Talmud, and it opens with the evening Shema.
reading: The Babylonian Talmud is arranged in six orders, and each order holds several tractates. A tractate is one book of the Mishnah and its Gemara. The very first tractate is called *Berakhot*, which means "blessings." It deals with prayers and blessings: the Shema, the standing prayer, and blessings said over food.

Berakhot opens with the *Shema*. The prayer takes its name from its first Hebrew word, "hear," in Deuteronomy 6:4. Rabbinic tradition holds that Jews recite it every evening and every morning. That practice comes from how the rabbis read Deuteronomy 6:7, which speaks of words said "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Why start the whole Talmud with the evening prayer and not the morning? The Gemara itself raises that question a little later on the page, as you will see. For now, notice the choice. The Talmud's first topic is a daily practice that ordinary people did at home. Law in this book begins with something close to everyday life.

words.d: one book of the Mishnah or Talmud, on one main subject
"blessings"; the first tractate of the Talmud, about prayers and blessings
a prayer made of verses from Deuteronomy, beginning "Hear, O Israel"; rabbinic tradition has it said evening and morning

look.title: A Daily Practice
look.text: Picture a home in Babylonia around 400 CE. The sun has set. A father finishes work and a child finishes chores. Before bed, both say the Shema. The rabbis ask: from what moment does "lying down" time begin?
look.prompt: Why might a book of law begin with a question that every household faced each night?

check.q: What does the name Berakhot mean?
check.why: Berakhot means "blessings"; the tractate deals with prayers and blessings.

check.q: Which prayer does the Talmud's first line discuss?
check.why: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 asks when the evening Shema may be said.

check.q: Which verse do the rabbis read as the source for saying the Shema at night and in the morning?
check.why: Deuteronomy 6:7 speaks of "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

lessons.title: Three Answers, All Kept
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 gives three different end times for the evening Shema and keeps every opinion.
reading: The Mishnah's first line reads, in paraphrase: from what time may one recite the Shema in the evening? From the hour when the priests go in to eat their *terumah*. Terumah was the gift of food that Israelites gave to priests. The Mishnah uses the priests' mealtime as a clock for the start of night.

Then come three end times. Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until the dawn rises. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Gamliel were leading teachers of the late first and early second centuries CE. "The Sages" means the majority of the teachers.

Notice what the Mishnah does. It does not name a winner in this line. It lists the voices side by side. Later Jewish law generally follows the Sages' midnight as the ideal, while treating dawn as the outer limit after the fact. Keeping the losing views is a habit you will see on almost every page. The Talmud treats a minority opinion as worth remembering.

words.d: the first written collection of rabbinic law, edited c. 200 CE
a food gift that Israelites gave to priests; priests could eat it only when ritually pure
in the Mishnah, the majority of the teachers, as opposed to one named rabbi

look.title: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1
look.text: From when may one read the Shema in the evening? From the hour the priests go in to eat their terumah, until the end of the first watch, says Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages say: until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: until dawn comes up.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 (Berakhot 2a), paraphrased from the Hebrew; compare Rodkinson's translation (1896–1903)
look.prompt: Which of the three opinions gives a person the most time? Why might a teacher want to keep all three?

check.q: In Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, what marks the start of the time for the evening Shema?
choices: When the priests go in to eat their terumah
check.why: The Mishnah uses the priests' evening meal of terumah as the marker of nightfall.

check.q: Which teacher says the evening Shema may be said until dawn?
check.why: Rabban Gamliel gives the latest limit, the rising of dawn.

check.q: What does the Mishnah do with the three different opinions?
choices: It crosses out the minority views
It lists them side by side and keeps them all
It picks Rabbi Eliezer as the only law
It says none of them matter
check.why: The Mishnah records all three voices, a habit the Talmud keeps throughout.

lessons.title: The Sons Come Home Late
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah tells how Rabban Gamliel's sons came home after midnight and he let them say the Shema, showing mercy inside the law.
reading: Right after the three opinions, the Mishnah tells a short story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home from a wedding feast after midnight. They told their father they had not yet said the Shema. The Sages had set midnight as the limit. Had the sons missed their chance?

Rabban Gamliel answered, in paraphrase: if dawn has not yet risen, you are still obligated to say it. Then the Mishnah explains the Sages' own view. When they said "until midnight," they meant it as a fence. A fence is a safety rule. It keeps a person far from breaking the real limit, so no one lazily waits until morning.

The story shows the course's second thread, mercy. The young men were not scolded for going to a wedding. They were given a way to keep the practice. It also shows the first thread, argument. The Mishnah does not just state a limit. It explains why a stricter limit was set. A reader learns both the rule and the reasoning that protects it.

words.d: in rabbinic law, an extra safeguard set around a rule so people do not come close to breaking it
required to do something by law
a celebration meal after a wedding; in the Mishnah, the reason the sons came home late

look.title: A Late Night
look.text: It is 1 a.m. Two brothers walk home from a friend's wedding. They remember the Shema. One says, "Too late, the Sages said midnight." The other says, "Let's ask Father."
look.prompt: Using Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, what would Rabban Gamliel say, and how does the idea of a fence explain his answer?

check.q: Why did Rabban Gamliel's sons come home late?
choices: They were at a wedding feast
check.why: The Mishnah says they came back from a wedding feast.

check.q: What does the Mishnah say the Sages meant by "until midnight"?
choices: It was the exact moment the law ends
It was a mistake they later took back
It was a fence to keep people far from the real limit
check.why: The Mishnah explains the Sages set midnight as a safeguard, while the true limit was dawn.

check.q: Which course thread does Rabban Gamliel's answer to his sons show most clearly?
choices: Mercy: he finds a way for them to keep the practice
A ruling that weddings are forbidden
check.why: He tells them they may still say the Shema before dawn, a merciful reading of the law.

lessons.title: The Gemara's First Question
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara opens by asking what earlier source the Mishnah's teacher assumed when he asked "from what time."
reading: The Gemara on Berakhot 2a begins with a short Aramaic question, often quoted as "tanna heikha kai?" It means "where does the *tanna* stand?" A tanna is a teacher from the time of the Mishnah. The question points at a hidden assumption. The Mishnah asks "from what time" as if everyone already knows there is a duty to say the Shema at night.

So where did that duty come from? The Gemara wants the root. This is a key move in almost every *sugya*. A sugya is one unit of Talmudic discussion on a topic. It often begins by asking for the source of a rule, the reason behind it, or the assumption it hides.

Readers across Jewish life notice this opening. Traditional yeshiva students learn to ask "where does the tanna stand?" as a habit. Academic scholars read it as a sign of how the editors of the Talmud worked: they tie each rule back to Scripture or to an earlier teaching. Both kinds of readers agree that the Gemara prizes questions.

words.d: the discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis, mostly in Aramaic, edited c. 500–600 CE
a teacher from the time of the Mishnah (to c. 200 CE)
one unit of Talmudic discussion on a single topic

look.title: Find the Hidden Assumption
look.text: Imagine a school rule that says, "From what time may students enter the library at lunch?" Before answering, a student asks, "Wait, where does it say students may use the library at lunch at all?"
look.prompt: How is this student's question like the Gemara's first question on Berakhot 2a?

check.q: What does the Gemara's first question, "where does the tanna stand?", ask?
choices: Where the teacher's house was located
What earlier source or assumption the Mishnah's teacher relied on
Whether the tanna was standing or sitting
Which city the Mishnah was written in
check.why: The question asks for the root of the duty the Mishnah takes for granted.

check.q: What is a sugya?
choices: One unit of Talmudic discussion on a topic
check.why: A sugya is a single discussion in the Gemara, with its questions and answers.

check.q: In what language is most of the Gemara written?
check.why: The Gemara is mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, while the Mishnah is in Hebrew.

lessons.title: Two Roots for One Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara offers two sources for the evening Shema: the verse about lying down, and the creation story's "evening and morning."
reading: The Gemara gives a first answer: the tanna stands on the verse. Deuteronomy 6:7 says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The rabbis read lying down as nighttime and rising up as morning. The duty exists because the verse says so, and the Mishnah just asks when it starts.

Then the Gemara adds a second possibility. Maybe the tanna learned it from the story of creation. Genesis 1:5 says, "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Evening comes first in the verse. So, the Gemara suggests, the Mishnah teaches the evening Shema first too.

This answers a question you met earlier. Why does the Talmud start with the evening and not the morning? The creation verse gives a reason: in the Hebrew Bible the day begins at evening. This is why Jewish holidays and Shabbat begin at sundown. Two proofs, one from law and one from creation, support the same rule.

words.d: in the Gemara, a verse or earlier teaching brought to support a claim
one numbered line of a biblical book, such as Deuteronomy 6:7
the first book of the Hebrew Bible, which tells of creation

look.title: The Verse Behind the Rule
look.text: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 6:7, The Holy Scriptures According to the Masoretic Text (Jewish Publication Society, 1917)
look.prompt: Which words in this verse do the rabbis read as "night" and "morning"?

check.q: Which verse does the Gemara use to explain why the Mishnah starts with evening?
choices: Genesis 1:5, "there was evening and there was morning"
check.why: Genesis 1:5 names evening before morning, so the Mishnah can begin with evening.

check.q: How do the rabbis read "when thou liest down" in Deuteronomy 6:7?
choices: As a rule about beds in the Temple
As the time for the nighttime Shema
As a command to rest on Shabbat
check.why: The rabbis link lying down with night and rising up with morning.

check.q: Why do Jewish holidays and Shabbat begin at sundown, according to this reading?
choices: Because the priests could not see in daylight
Because the Mishnah forgot the morning
Because in Genesis 1 evening comes before morning
check.why: The creation account lists evening first, and rabbinic tradition counts the day from evening.

lessons.title: Priests and Stars
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara reads the priests' mealtime as a sign of nightfall, the time when the stars come out.
reading: Why does the Mishnah use priests eating terumah as its clock? The Gemara explains through a verse in Leviticus 22:7. A priest who became ritually impure had to immerse in water. Then, in the verse, when the sun is down he is clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy food.

So the priests went in to eat their terumah once night had truly come. The Gemara connects that moment with the appearance of the stars. Later Jewish practice still uses the phrase *tzeit ha-kokhavim*, "the coming out of the stars," to mark nightfall. Many Jewish calendars print this time each day.

Here the Gemara reads the Mishnah's words as a code. The Mishnah could have said "when the stars come out." Instead it named a practice from the Temple, which had been destroyed in 70 CE by the time the Mishnah was edited. Some readers say this kept the memory of the Temple alive in daily prayer. Others see it simply as a well-known sign of night.

words.d: in biblical law, a status that kept a person from holy food or places until purified
"the coming out of the stars"; the rabbinic marker of nightfall
to go fully under water to become ritually pure

look.title: A Clock Without a Clock
look.text: There are no wristwatches in the ancient world. You need a sign that everyone can see or know. One teacher names the priests' dinner. Another might name the first three stars in the sky.
look.prompt: What makes a good public sign of nightfall? Why might the Mishnah choose one tied to the Temple?

check.q: According to the Gemara's reading of Leviticus 22:7, when could a purified priest eat terumah?
choices: At noon on the next day
check.why: The verse says once the sun is down he is clean and may eat holy food.

check.q: What does tzeit ha-kokhavim mean?
choices: The coming out of the stars
The first watch of the night
check.why: It is the rabbinic phrase for nightfall, marked by visible stars.

check.q: By the time the Mishnah was edited, what had happened to the Temple in Jerusalem?
choices: It had been destroyed in 70 CE
It was being run by the Sages
check.why: The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, over a century before the Mishnah (c. 200 CE).

lessons.title: The Poor Man's Dinner
lessons.mainIdea: A teaching quoted in the Gemara marks nightfall by when a poor person sits down to bread and salt.
reading: The Gemara on Berakhot 2b brings a *baraita*. A baraita is a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it. This baraita offers a different sign for the start of the evening Shema. It says: from the time a poor person comes in to eat bread with salt.

The Gemara then compares this sign with the priests' sign. Are they the same moment or not? The Gemara tests one against the other, asking which comes earlier. It even brings a third opinion about when people sit down to their Friday night meal. The discussion goes back and forth, and not every question is neatly closed.

Readers notice who is used as the clock here. First it was priests, the most honored class. Now it is the poor, who worked until dark and ate the simplest meal. Some teachers point out that the Talmud puts the poor worker's evening on the same page as the priest's. The rule about prayer quietly records how ordinary people lived.

words.d: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was left out of the Mishnah itself
a challenge in the Gemara that shows a problem with a claim
the simple meal of a poor laborer in the Talmud's world

look.title: Two Clocks for One Night
look.text: Clock A: when the priests go in to eat holy food. Clock B: when a poor worker comes home to eat bread and salt. The Gemara asks whether these two clocks show the same time.
look.prompt: Why might the time differ for priests and for a poor worker? What does it show that both are on the page?

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A teaching from the Mishnah's era that is not in the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is an outside tannaitic teaching the Gemara quotes.

check.q: What sign of nightfall does the baraita on Berakhot 2b give?
choices: When a poor person comes in to eat bread with salt
check.why: The baraita uses the poor man's simple evening meal as its marker.

check.q: What does the Gemara do with the priests' sign and the poor man's sign?
choices: It compares them to see whether they match
It ignores the poor man's sign
check.why: The Gemara tests one teaching against another, a typical move in a sugya.

lessons.title: Three Watches or Four?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara records a disagreement over whether the night has three watches or four, and gives signs for each.
reading: The Mishnah's Rabbi Eliezer said "until the end of the first watch." So the Gemara on Berakhot 3a asks: how many watches does the night have? A watch is a shift of the night, like a guard's turn. Rabbi Eliezer holds there are three. Rabbi Natan, another tanna, holds there are four.

The Gemara adds signs for each watch in Rabbi Eliezer's view. In the first watch, a donkey brays. In the second, dogs bark. In the third, a baby nurses at its mother's breast and a wife talks with her husband. These are sounds anyone in an ancient village would know. The Gemara also records an *aggadah* there: at each watch God roars like a lion, grieving over the Temple.

Here law and story sit side by side. A question about timing leads to a picture of a whole village at night, and to a teaching about sorrow for the destroyed Temple. Readers have long found this mix typical of the Talmud. The book moves easily from a legal detail to a scene of grief and back.

words.d: one part of the night, like a guard's shift
the story and teaching parts of the Talmud, as opposed to law
a tanna who, in Berakhot 3a, holds the night has four watches

look.title: Dividing a Twelve-Hour Night
look.cite: Berakhot 3a, as discussed by the Gemara; rounded to equal hours
look.prompt: If Rabbi Eliezer's first watch ends after four of twelve hours, how much of the night does his view leave for the evening Shema?

check.q: How many watches does Rabbi Eliezer say the night has, in Berakhot 3a?
check.why: Rabbi Eliezer counts three watches; Rabbi Natan counts four.

check.q: Which sign does the Gemara give for the second watch?
check.why: In the Gemara's list, dogs bark in the second watch.

check.q: What is aggadah?
choices: The legal rulings of the Talmud
A list of the night watches
The story and teaching parts of the Talmud
check.why: Aggadah is the Talmud's narrative and ethical material; halakhah is its law.

lessons.title: David's Harp at Midnight
lessons.mainIdea: On Berakhot 3b the Gemara tells that a harp over King David's bed played at midnight and woke him to study, linked to Psalm 119:62.
reading: A little further on, the Gemara turns to midnight. It quotes a verse from Psalms, which tradition credits to King David: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto Thee." How did David know the exact moment of midnight? The Gemara on Berakhot 3b answers with a story.

A harp hung above David's bed. When midnight came, a north wind blew through its strings and it played by itself. David would rise and study Torah until dawn. The story is aggadah. It is a picture of a king who set aside part of every night for learning.

Readers take this story in different ways. Some traditional readers hold it as a true account of David. Many modern and academic readers treat it as a teaching image about devotion and study. Rashi, the great commentator from France (1040–1105), explains details of the scene. All these readers agree the story ties the question of time to a love of learning.

words.d: a book of the Hebrew Bible made of songs and prayers; tradition credits many to King David
the middle of the night; in the Mishnah, the Sages' limit for the evening Shema
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of France, the best-known commentator on the Talmud

look.title: A Verse About Midnight
look.text: At midnight I rise to give thanks to You, because of Your righteous rulings.
look.cite: Psalm 119:62, paraphrased; cited in Berakhot 3b. Compare the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: How does the Gemara use this verse to connect midnight, David and study?

check.q: What made David's harp play at midnight, in the Gemara's story?
choices: A north wind blowing through its strings
check.why: Berakhot 3b says a north wind blew on the harp at midnight.

check.q: What did David do after the harp woke him, in the story?
check.why: The story pictures David rising to study through the rest of the night.

check.q: How do many modern academic readers treat the harp story?
choices: As a law about buying harps
As a proof that the Shema is said at noon
As a teaching image about devotion and study
As a mistake by the printers
check.why: Readers differ: some take it as history, many read it as an aggadic image.

lessons.title: Rodkinson Against the Page
lessons.mainIdea: Michael Rodkinson's English Talmud (1896–1903) is public domain and readable, but it is partial and abridged, so readers check it against the page.
reading: Most students first meet the Talmud in translation. One of the earliest English versions was made by Michael L. Rodkinson and published in New York from 1896 to 1903. Because it is old, it is now in the public domain. That means anyone may copy and share it freely. It is easy to find online.

Rodkinson's version has real strengths. It was one of the first attempts to put Talmud tractates into plain English for general readers. But scholars point out its gaps. It is partial, since it covers only some tractates. It is abridged, since Rodkinson shortened and rearranged passages. Its quality is uneven from volume to volume.

So a careful reader compares. Put Rodkinson's lines next to the Hebrew and Aramaic page, or next to a modern translation such as the Steinsaltz or Schottenstein editions or the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria. Those modern versions are not public domain, so they are cited and paraphrased. Ask: did the translator skip a step of the argument? Checking translations is part of reading closely.

words.d: no longer under copyright; free for anyone to copy and share
shortened, with parts left out
a text carried from one language into another

look.title: English Talmud Translations Over Time
look.cite: Publication dates as commonly given for the Rodkinson (New York) and Soncino (London) translations
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the end of Rodkinson and the start of Soncino? Why might a newer, fuller translation have been wanted?

check.q: Why may students freely quote Rodkinson's translation?
choices: It was written by the Mishnah's editors
It is the only translation that exists
It was printed in the Vilna Shas
It is in the public domain
check.why: Rodkinson's work (1896–1903) is old enough to be out of copyright.

check.q: Which is a known weakness of Rodkinson's translation?
choices: It is abridged and covers only part of the Talmud
It is written only in Aramaic
It was banned in the United States
check.why: Scholars note it is partial, shortened and uneven.

check.q: Why must the Soncino and Sefaria's William Davidson translations be paraphrased here?
choices: They are too old to read
They are not in the public domain
check.why: Both are still under copyright or restrictive licenses, so this course paraphrases them.

lessons.title: Mapping the Moves
lessons.mainIdea: Reading Berakhot 2a as a map of moves — question, proof, second proof, test — shows how a sugya works.
reading: Now put the pieces together as a map. First comes the Mishnah: a question and three opinions. Next the Gemara asks for the root: where does the tanna stand? Then come two proofs, one from Deuteronomy 6:7 and one from Genesis 1:5. After that the Gemara tests signs of nightfall, the priests and the poor man, against each other.

Each step has a name students can learn. A *kushya* is a hard question or objection. A *terutz* is an answer that resolves it. "Mai ta'ama?" means "what is the reason?" When the Gemara cannot settle a point, it may say *teyku*, "let it stand." Learning these names helps you see the shape under the words.

Many Jewish students learn these moves with a *chavruta*, a study partner. Partners read aloud, argue, and push each other to explain. Orthodox yeshivas, Conservative and Reform schools, and university classes all use partner study in different ways. The goal is the same: to follow the argument and to see what each step protects.

words.d: a hard question or objection in the Gemara
an answer that resolves an objection
a study partner, or the practice of studying Talmud in pairs
"let it stand"; the Gemara's word when a question stays unresolved

look.title: Label the Steps
look.text: 1) The Mishnah asks when the evening Shema begins. 2) The Gemara asks what the teacher assumed. 3) It answers with Deuteronomy 6:7. 4) It offers Genesis 1:5 instead. 5) It compares the priests' sign with the poor man's sign.
look.prompt: Label each step as question, proof or test. Which step would you call the turning point?

check.q: What is a kushya?
check.why: A kushya is the Gemara's objection; a terutz answers it.

check.q: What does teyku mean?
choices: Let it stand; the question stays open
check.why: Teyku marks a question the Gemara leaves unresolved.

check.q: What is a chavruta?
choices: A study partner, or studying in pairs
check.why: Chavruta study pairs learners who read and argue together.

review.q: Which tractate opens the Babylonian Talmud?
What is the Talmud's first question about its first Mishnah?
review.why: The Gemara on Berakhot 2a asks what source the Mishnah's teacher assumed.

review.q: Which three voices give end times for the evening Shema in Mishnah Berakhot 1:1?
choices: Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages and Rabban Gamliel
review.why: The Mishnah lists Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages and Rabban Gamliel.

review.q: Why does the Gemara suggest the Mishnah begins with evening?
choices: The priests worked only at night
The Shema has no morning version
review.why: The creation verse lists evening first.

review.q: What does the Mishnah say the Sages' midnight limit was?
choices: A fence to keep people far from the real limit
The exact end of the law
review.why: The Mishnah explains the midnight limit as a safeguard.

review.q: Which pair of signs for nightfall does the Gemara compare?
choices: The donkey braying and the dogs barking
The harp playing and the dawn rising
The priests eating terumah and the poor man eating bread with salt
The Temple gates and the city walls
review.why: The Gemara tests the priests' sign against the baraita's poor man sign.

review.q: In Berakhot 3b, what woke King David at midnight?
choices: A harp played by the north wind
review.why: The Gemara tells of a harp over David's bed that played at midnight.

review.q: What should a careful reader do with Rodkinson's translation?
choices: Check it against the page or a modern translation
Treat it as complete and exact
Ignore it because it is in English
Use it only for Rashi's notes
review.why: Rodkinson's version is abridged and uneven, so readers compare it with the page.
